title: Practical Work with the Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads essays from David Rynick's book This Truth Never Fails, opening with "First Day Back," where an anxious morning mind is a young dog sniffing every bush and a memory of a kayak on Maine's Medomak River brings comfort. Nomon adds five suggestions from a Seattle mindfulness class for young doctors: be friendly with the crazy mind, attend to posture, slow down a little, see thoughts as thoughts, and practice formally each day. More essays follow, including "Reluctant Adventurer" and an Ango breakdown that ends with asking others for help. After conversations in pairs, the room turns to doctors dreading the pager on call, and one who left residency over stubborn bodily tension.

*Monday morning, I wake up groggy after a week's vacation.
It's only 5:30.
No need to get up yet.
I doze lightly until six, when the urge to pee becomes irresistible.
I shuffle to the bathroom, do my business, and slip back between the sheets. [unclear: "Good night, and"] the warm air already feels oppressive.

There's no drifting back to sleep this morning, so I lay here at the beginning of my day, in the middle of my life, and work with my brain that has already begun to scan the horizon for news of trouble.*
*As usual, there's an abundance available.
My anxious morning mind is like a young dog out for a walk.
Every tree and every bush must be investigated to find out who's peed there and what the news is.
The objects of my worrying investigation this morning are many.

The garden is running wild, so many things to be tied up or weeded or dug up and moved, the to-do list in preparation for the next retreat, and the workers that may or may not be coming today to repair the newly discovered leak in the roof.
Then there's my life coaching business.
Do I have enough clients?
Will the next workshop really happen?
And I really should have replaced my website years ago.
I can usually ignore this undone task, but this morning I can't seem to stay away from it.*
*Like a kindly yet firm owner, I allow my doggy mind to sniff around and try to keep him moving.
I prevent him from engaging in this low-class sniffing behavior if I could, but we've had that battle for years, and he, my mind, always wins.
So this morning, using my firmest and not angry-at-all owner's voice, I say, we're not going to spend ten minutes on each smell, or each worrisome thought that comes by.
So we explore briefly and keep moving.
I notice that it's the same everywhere I look.
This morning, everything I encounter is evidence of my deficiency and the impending falling apart of my life.
That's the theme.*
*But stepping back even just a little, I admire the brilliance of this mind state.
The anxious mind manifests an unshakable confidence that what it is seeing is the truth.
No soft liberal relativism here.
This part of me is sure that he's exactly right about everything.
And from this confidence, an endless creativity arises.
Everything that arises is used to bolster the argument.
Every new observation is used to further support the perspective that the world is a worrisome place, and I'm deep in real trouble now.*
*My strategy this morning is to keep trying not to get totally hooked into one problem, to keep my doggy mind moving.
And while I'm still partly asleep, I scan for other ways of working with this worried mind, strategies that might be helpful.
I look for images or feelings or dreams that might be lurking in the corner.
In my mind, I come across an image of my hands moving in a way that reminds me of the flow of the flood tide coming up the Medomak River of coastal Maine.
While this overall direction is clear and powerful, the tide is irresistibly coming in.
The movement of the water in any particular place is chaotic and turbulent.
Eddies and microcurrents flow in every direction.*
*Two months ago, I sat in my kayak near the mouth of this river.
The tide is full flood, and the water beneath my boat seems to be flowing in many directions at once.
I imagine that if every current were visible, it would look like an intricate paisley pattern of interlocking curls.
Floating in my kayak, I let the gentle currents push me around, spinning the boat, taking me first one direction, then the other.
For some reason, this image, this memory, is comforting to me.
Maybe all these worries are just the many currents of my life.
Perhaps there is a larger direction which holds it all.
What if I could trust the deeper flow, and just allow the boat of myself to turn with the current?
I raise my hand to my face and touch my cheek.
There, there, I say to myself.
Everything will be just fine.*
*I am almost surprised to find the stubble from my beard.
The scared little boy is actually a man, who still needs comfort and reassurance on this first morning back in the saddle of his work life after vacation.
And then I think of how much I love to ride horses.
The beauty and power of their galloping aliveness.
Ah, the trustworthy energy of life in its many forms.
Now I remember.*
